pedagogy.summary: Children learn to compare and sort a mixed collection of 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects by their geometric PROPERTIES — number of sides, number/type of faces, flat vs curved surfaces, number of vertices — and to articulate the criterion they used. The procedural goal is a consistent, property-based sort: choosing one attribute, applying it to every item, and being able to re-sort the same collection a different way. It builds directly on knowing the properties (2-D sides, 3-D faces/edges/vertices) and pushes children off the van Hiele visual level, where they group by overall look, colour or size. Best taught with real shapes to handle, 'is/is not' two-set sorting, and 'guess my rule' games.
bestPractices: Sort a physical, mixed collection into two sets on an 'is / is not' criterion (e.g. has a curved surface / has no curved surface), then challenge children to re-sort the SAME set a different way.
Play 'guess my rule': present a set already sorted by someone else and have children infer the property used — this makes the criterion explicit.
Insist the rule is a geometric property; when a child groups by colour or size, restrict the set to one colour/size so appearance cannot be the criterion.
Hand children real solids to handle and mark faces/edges/vertices with a wipe-clean pen as they count, so a sort by 'number of faces' rests on an accurate count.
Model articulating the rule aloud ('all of these have a triangular face') and ask 'does EVERY shape in this group follow your rule?' to check consistency.
keyRepresentations: A mixed tray of handleable 2-D shapes and 3-D solids plus everyday objects
Two sorting hoops / Carroll or Venn two-set frame labelled with an 'is / is not' criterion
Wipe-clean pen for marking faces/edges/vertices while counting
commonMisconceptions: Sorts by a non-defining feature — colour, size or overall look — rather than a geometric property.
Groups shapes by holistic resemblance ('these look the same') and cannot state a single consistent rule, letting the rule drift mid-sort.
Miscounts sides, faces or vertices — losing track of where counting started — so shapes end up in the wrong group.
Can sort one way but cannot re-sort the same collection by a different property, or cannot infer the rule of a set sorted by someone else.

learn.summary: Children aged 6-7 learn to compare and sort a mixed collection of 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects by geometric PROPERTIES — number of sides, number/type of faces, flat vs curved surfaces, number of vertices — and to articulate the criterion used. The procedural goal is a consistent, property-based sort: choose one attribute, apply it to every item, then re-sort the SAME collection a different way. This builds on knowing the properties and pushes children off the van Hiele visual level, where they group by overall look, colour or size. Best taught with real shapes to handle, 'is / is not' two-set sorting, and 'guess my rule' games.

activities.title: Sort a real tray two ways on an 'is / is not' rule
feedback: If a child groups by colour, size or 'the pretty ones', restrict the collection to a single colour and size so appearance cannot be the criterion, forcing attention to a property.

When a placement breaks the chosen rule (e.g. a cone, which has a curved surface, dropped into 'no curved surface'), point to the mismatch and ask which property decides membership — the property, not the look.
Prompt consistency: 'Does every shape in this group follow your rule?' If membership drifts for a borderline shape, revisit the stated rule.

Watching a shape such as a triangular prism move to the other hoop when the rule changes — it has no curved surface but does have triangular faces, so it belongs in a different group under each rule — is the moment 'a sort needs one property' becomes concrete. (A cube would stay put, since it has neither a curved surface nor a triangular face.)
activities.rationale: 'Is / is not' two-set sorting with a required second re-sort of the same set targets the flexible, property-based sorting that distinguishes a child reading shapes by property from one grouping by overall look. Restricting colour/size removes appearance as a possible criterion.
sourceClaims: Children should sort shapes into two sets on 'is / is not' criteria and be able to guess a sorting rule from how shapes have been sorted; a common misconception is failing to recognise a shape in a different orientation, remedied by handling and rotating cut-outs.

Young children at the van Hiele visualization level group shapes holistically by appearance, colour and orientation rather than defining properties; the instructional goal is to analyse shapes by properties (e.g. number of sides), invariant to colour, size and orientation.
learnerActions: Take a physical, mixed tray of handleable 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects.

Choose ONE geometric property as the rule (e.g. 'has a curved surface / has no curved surface') and place every item into one of two sorting hoops or a labelled two-set frame. Check that the rule makes sense for every item in the tray: a flat 2-D shape such as a circle has a curved side (edge) but no curved surface, so either agree how 2-D shapes are judged or pick a rule that fits both 2-D and 3-D items (e.g. 'has a curved edge or surface / has none').
Say the rule aloud ('all of these have a curved surface') and check: does EVERY shape in this group follow my rule?
Now scatter the SAME shapes and re-sort them by a different property (e.g. 'has a triangular face / has no triangular face'); notice which shapes move to a different hoop and why.
activities.intendedInsight: A sort rests on one geometric property held constant and applied to every item; the same collection can be grouped validly in more than one way depending on which property you choose.

activities.title: Guess my rule
feedback: If a child cannot state a single rule that every group member satisfies, model one aloud ('these all have a triangular face') and check each member against it.

If the inferred rule is a non-geometric feature such as colour or size, point to two members of the SAME group that differ in that named feature (e.g. two different colours) yet were grouped together, so the child sees appearance cannot be the rule and looks for the shared geometric property.
Confirm success when the child's continuation placements all satisfy the same stated property.
activities.rationale: Inferring someone else's rule separates a child who reads shapes by property from one who grouped by holistic resemblance; it makes the criterion explicit rather than letting it drift.
sourceClaims: Children should sort shapes into two sets on 'is / is not' criteria and be able to guess a sorting rule from how shapes have been sorted; a common misconception is failing to recognise a shape in a different orientation, remedied by handling and rotating cut-outs.
learnerActions: Look at a set someone else has already sorted into two groups, with the rule hidden.
Infer and state the geometric property that was used to make the two groups.
Continue the sort by placing a few more shapes into the correct group, keeping the rule constant.
Then set your own 'guess my rule' challenge for a partner.
activities.intendedInsight: Making the hidden criterion explicit forces attention onto defining properties and shows that a good sort rests on one rule every member satisfies.

activities.title: Count faces, edges and vertices accurately before sorting
feedback: If recounts give different totals, ask how to be sure each side/face is counted once and model marking each one as it is counted — scaffold the counting, do not reteach the whole topic.
If a shape lands in the wrong group, check whether its faces/vertices were miscounted rather than whether the rule was wrong.
activities.rationale: Miscounting sides, faces or vertices from losing track of the starting point is a known error that makes count-based sorts inconsistent; handling real solids and marking each feature addresses the difficulty of counting features from an image.
sourceClaims: 3-D shapes can be sorted by their properties (faces, edges, vertices; e.g. curved surface / no curved surface, 6-or-more vertices, no triangular faces); the stated common misconception is that children find it hard to count faces, vertices and edges from an IMAGE of a solid; remedy is to hand children real solids to handle and mark each feature with a wipe-clean pen as they count.

A common misconception is that children miscount sides or vertices because they lose track of where they started counting; the remedy is to ask how to count each side/vertex once and model marking each one as it is counted.
learnerActions: Hold a real solid and mark each face, edge or vertex with a wipe-clean pen as you count it, so you count each one exactly once.
Record the count, then use it as the sorting rule (e.g. 'sort solids by number of faces' or 'six or more vertices / fewer than six vertices').
Recount a solid a second way and check you get the same total; if not, find where you lost track.
Place each solid in the correct group based on the verified count.
activities.intendedInsight: A count-based sort is only as reliable as the count; marking each feature once prevents losing track and keeps the sort consistent.

activities.title: Inspect 3-D solids for flat vs curved surfaces
feedback: If a child decides from one view only, prompt them to turn the solid right over to check the other surfaces.
Confirm when the flat-vs-curved judgement matches every surface inspected (e.g. a cylinder has two flat circular faces and one curved surface).
activities.rationale: Handling and rotating solids helps children judge flat-vs-curved surfaces that are hard to read from a static image. An on-screen rotatable solid may supplement this for the 3-D portion, though the sorting action itself is a flat grouping task; efficacy relative to handling is untested here.
sourceClaims: 3-D shapes can be sorted by their properties (faces, edges, vertices; e.g. curved surface / no curved surface, 6-or-more vertices, no triangular faces); the stated common misconception is that children find it hard to count faces, vertices and edges from an IMAGE of a solid; remedy is to hand children real solids to handle and mark each feature with a wipe-clean pen as they count.
learnerActions: Pick up and rotate each solid to inspect every surface, feeling and looking for flat versus curved surfaces.
Sort the solids into 'has a curved surface / has no curved surface' based on what you found.
Explain for a tricky solid (e.g. a cylinder) which surfaces are flat and which are curved.
activities.intendedInsight: Rotating a solid to inspect all its surfaces reveals properties that a single view hides, supporting an accurate flat-vs-curved sort.

constraints: The skill is doing: placing shapes, testing a criterion, and re-sorting. A view-only tap-to-reveal illustration does not let the child perform or switch a sort, so it does not build the procedure on its own.

A fixed, scored categorization (sort by a GIVEN rule) can check sorting against a supplied criterion, but because the rule is provided it does not require the child to choose, articulate or switch the criterion; use it to check rather than to build the flexible re-sort.
Insist the rule is a geometric property; when a child groups by colour or size, restrict the set to one colour/size so appearance cannot be the criterion.
Require a SECOND, different sort of the same collection plus a 'guess my rule' inference — these are what best separate property-based sorting from grouping by overall look.

Paper or card cut-outs and real solids have slight thickness and can be held and turned; treat them as physical representations of the mathematical shapes, and ask children about the shape REPRESENTED, not whether the object can be picked up. A rotatable on-screen solid is a model that may supplement, not replace, handling where handling is available.

When naming a specific solid in an example, make sure it fits the property claimed (e.g. use a triangular prism/pyramid when illustrating 'has a triangular face', and only call a solid a cube when it is cube-shaped); do not assume a generic box is a cube.

An optional on-screen drag-into-two-loops sorter with a swappable rule tile and immediate feedback (a shape springing back with a red outline when it breaks the rule) can make the mechanism concrete; this is one possible interaction, not a required one, and its benefit over physical sorting is untested.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy 'poor / ideal / possible' artefact rankings and the claim that a conversation 'adds nothing' were catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical facts; they have been reframed as scoped affordances/limits (e.g. view-only media do not support the active sorting that is the objective). No claim of medium superiority is asserted beyond these narrow affordances.

The original research narrative used a CUBE as the shape that 'moves to the other hoop' when switching from 'has a curved surface' to 'has a triangular face'. A cube has neither a curved surface nor a triangular face, so under the natural relabelling it stays in the 'no' group for both rules and does not move. This has been corrected in the activity to a shape that genuinely moves (e.g. a triangular prism).
'Six or more vertices' as a sorting band is taken from the source example; confirm the solids provided actually make this discrimination meaningful for the specific collection used.
The first 'guess my rule' set must itself be sorted by a valid single geometric property, or the inference task is unsound; check the pre-sorted example before use.

probeDeeper: You put these together — tell me your rule. Does EVERY shape in this group follow it?
Can you sort exactly the same shapes a completely different way?
I'll add this shape [a large, differently-coloured triangle] — which group does it go in, and why?
Here is a set I sorted into two groups. What was my rule?
assess.correctAnswer: Sorts by a stated geometric property — e.g. 2-D shapes by number of sides, or 3-D solids by flat-vs-curved faces or number of faces/vertices — applies it consistently to every shape, articulates the rule ('these all have a curved surface'), re-sorts the same collection by a different property, and infers the property behind a set sorted by someone else.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sorts by a non-defining feature — colour, size or 'the pretty ones' — rather than a geometric property.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Restrict the collection to a single colour and size so appearance cannot be the criterion, forcing attention to a property; model a property rule aloud ('I'm putting all the ones with a curved surface here').
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The two groups differ by colour or size, not by sides/faces; when asked the rule, the child names a non-geometric feature.

errorPatterns.pattern: Groups by holistic resemblance ('these look the same') without an explicit criterion, and the rule drifts as more shapes are added.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Play 'guess my rule' with a pre-sorted set, then have the child continue that sort — modelling that a sort rests on one explicit property held constant.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Cannot state a single rule that every group member satisfies; membership changes when asked to justify a borderline shape.

errorPatterns.pattern: Miscounts sides, faces or vertices because they lose track of where they started, so a count-based sort is inconsistent.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold, don't reteach: ask how to be sure each side/face is counted once, and model marking each one with a wipe-clean pen as it is counted.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Recounts give different totals; a shape lands in the wrong group because its sides/faces were miscounted.

responseLevels.gap: Sorts by a non-geometric feature (colour, size) or by holistic resemblance, cannot state a consistent rule, or miscounts so the sort is wrong.
responseLevels.full: Sorts by a stated geometric property applied consistently to every shape, re-sorts the same collection by a different property, and infers the rule of a set sorted by someone else — treating number of sides / flat-vs-curved faces / number of vertices as the basis for grouping (SOLO relational, with transfer).
responseLevels.partial: Sorts correctly by one property and states that rule, but cannot re-sort the collection a different way, applies the rule inconsistently to some shapes, or cannot infer the rule of a pre-sorted set (SOLO multistructural — one criterion, not coordinated).

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a mixed tray of 2-D shapes and 3-D solids. Set the task and watch: 'Sort these into two groups so that everything in a group shares something. When you are done, tell me your rule.' Then: 'Now sort the same shapes a completely different way.' Finally, hand them a set you have already sorted and say: 'What was my rule?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the sort (rather than asking the child to describe sorting) reveals whether the criterion is a defining property applied consistently, or an appearance feature / a rule that drifts. Requiring a SECOND, different sort of the same shapes and a 'guess my rule' inference separates a child who reads shapes by property from one who grouped by overall look — the latter can rarely re-sort or name someone else's rule.
